misconceptions.description: Takes the first time mentioned and ignores the correction

misconceptions.description: Confuses quarter past and quarter to

teachingSuccessCriteria: Finds the final time after a correction
Converts half past, quarter past and quarter to into clock times

lesson.title: What time is it?
lesson.objective: Identify the final time agreed in a short written dialogue, including changed times and quarter/half past or to.

objectives: Identify the final time agreed in a short written dialogue, including changed times and quarter/half past or to.
successCriteria: Finds the final time after a correction
Converts half past, quarter past and quarter to into clock times
examples: A: Is the class at nine? B: No, at ten.
A: Meet at quarter to two. B: OK.

items.material: A: Is the lesson at five? B: No, it is at six.
A: See you at quarter past two. B: Great, quarter past two.

outcomes.studyNotes: When people talk about times, listen for corrections. Often the first time is wrong and the speaker changes it: "Is it at five?" "No, at six." The answer is six, the last time. Learn the clock words: half past four is 4:30. Quarter past four is 4:15. Quarter to five is 4:45, because it is fifteen minutes before five. Words like "No", "Actually" and "I mean" show a change. Read the whole dialogue before you answer.

scriptedTutor.explanation: In a dialogue the final agreed time is the answer. A correction such as "No, at six" replaces the first time. Quarter past means 15 minutes after the hour; quarter to means 15 minutes before the next hour.
hints: Which time do both speakers accept at the end?
Look for the word No or Actually; it changes the time.
Quarter to is before the hour, quarter past is after.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Read the dialogue again and look at the last thing the speakers agree on.
scriptedTutor.closing: Well done. Always check the last time mentioned.

lesson.title: How much is it?
lesson.objective: Pick out prices and quantities in a short written dialogue, telling apart pairs such as 13/30 and 15/50.

objectives: Pick out prices and quantities in a short written dialogue, telling apart pairs such as 13/30 and 15/50.
successCriteria: Finds the price actually paid after a discount or change

items.material: A: How much is the bag? B: It is sixteen dollars.

items.prompt: How much does the cap cost now?
items.material: A: The cap was 20 dollars. B: Now it is 15 dollars.

outcomes.studyNotes: Numbers ending in -teen (13 to 19) and -ty (30 to 90) sound and look similar. Thirteen is 13 but thirty is 30. Fourteen is 14 but forty is 40. Fifteen is 15 and fifty is 50. In writing look at the ending: -teen means 1 plus a number, -ty means tens. In shops, prices can change: "It was 20, now 15." Choose the price that the buyer will pay now. Words like now, today, sale and new show the final price.

scriptedTutor.explanation: -teen numbers are 13 to 19; -ty numbers are tens like 30 and 40. When a price changes, the price to pay is the new price, after words like now or today.
hints: Does the number end in -teen or -ty?
Which price is the new one?
Check the number words one letter at a time.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Read the dialogue again and look at the last thing the speakers agree on.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Check -teen versus -ty and the new price.

lesson.title: Making plans
lesson.objective: Find specific details (person, place, day) in a short written conversation, including details that change.

objectives: Find specific details (person, place, day) in a short written conversation, including details that change.
successCriteria: Finds the final place or day agreed
Connects each detail to the right speaker
examples: A: Let's meet at the park. B: How about the cafe? A: OK, the cafe.

outcomes.studyNotes: Detail questions ask who, where or when. Read the whole dialogue because people often change plans. A place mentioned first may be rejected: "At the cafe?" "No, let's go to the library." The answer is the library. Words that show rejection are no, not, rather, instead and but. Words that show agreement are OK, fine, good idea and sure. For who questions, check the speaker before each sentence: A said it or B said it. Then match the detail to the correct person.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Detail questions need the final agreed place, day or person. Notice rejection words and agreement words, and check which speaker said each sentence.
hints: Which place do both speakers finally choose?
Does the speaker say no, instead or but?
Who is speaking in that sentence, A or B?
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Read the dialogue again and look at the last thing the speakers agree on.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Find the final plan and the right speaker.

objectives: Decide whether a speaker agrees or refuses an offer or request, including polite and indirect refusals.
successCriteria: Decides agree or refuse from the whole reply

items.prompt: Does B agree or refuse? Write agree or refuse.
items.material: A: Can you come tonight? B: I'm sorry, I'm busy.

outcomes.studyNotes: In dialogues people often say no in a polite way. Words like sorry, I'm afraid, I'd love to but and thanks but can show a refusal. Thanks alone does not always mean yes. Agreement words are sure, of course, OK, great and with pleasure. Be careful: a reply can start with a positive word and then end with "but". "Yes, but I have to work" is usually a refusal. Read to the end of the reply and decide: does the person do what was asked, or not?

scriptedTutor.explanation: Read the whole reply. Polite words may start a refusal. The reasons after but, sorry or I'm afraid usually show that the answer is no.
hints: Read to the end of the reply.
Does the speaker give a reason why they cannot?
Words like sure and of course show agreement.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Read the dialogue again and look at the last thing the speakers agree on.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Listen for the final meaning, not just polite words.

lesson.title: What are they talking about?
lesson.objective: Name the general topic of a short written dialogue from key words, without relying on one word alone.

objectives: Name the general topic of a short written dialogue from key words, without relying on one word alone.
successCriteria: Uses several clues to decide the main topic
Separates the main subject from side details
examples: A: I have a headache and a fever. B: You should see a doctor. (health)

items.prompt: What is the topic: money, weather or food?
items.material: A: How much is left in my account? B: Fifty dollars, so no shopping this week.

outcomes.studyNotes: To find the topic of a dialogue, ask: what are both speakers talking about most? One word is not enough. A dialogue with the word "breakfast" may be about a hotel, not about food. Look for a group of clues. Words like doctor, fever and medicine suggest health. Words like ticket, airport and delay suggest travel. Words like salary, boss and meeting suggest work. Side details appear once; the main topic returns in many lines. After you choose, check: does your topic explain every line of the dialogue?

scriptedTutor.explanation: The topic is the subject that explains most of the lines. Gather several clue words and do not choose from just one word.
hints: Which words belong to the same group?
Does your topic explain every line?
Ignore details mentioned only once.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Read the dialogue again and look at the last thing the speakers agree on.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Use a group of clue words to find the topic.

lesson.title: Giving and following directions
lesson.objective: Follow step-by-step directions and instructions in a short written dialogue to find a final place or action.

objectives: Follow step-by-step directions and instructions in a short written dialogue to find a final place or action.
successCriteria: Follows each step in order to the final place

A: First open the box. B: Then?

items.material: A: Go straight, take the first left. The post office is on the corner. B: Thanks.

items.prompt: What does B do after turning right?
items.material: A: Turn right at the lights, then walk to the end of the street. B: OK.
acceptedAnswers: walk to the end of the street

outcomes.studyNotes: Directions come in steps. Each step changes your position, so follow them in order. "Take the second left" means pass the first street on the left, then turn into the next one. Sequence words are first, then, next, after that and finally. A place may also be described by its position: opposite, next to, behind or at the end. Imagine a map and move your finger on it. The answer is where you are after the last step, not after the first one. For instructions, such as cooking or using a machine, also do the steps in order.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Follow each step in order. Count streets carefully and use the last step as your final position.
hints: What is the last instruction?
Count the streets: second means skip one.
Draw a simple map as you read.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Read the dialogue again and look at the last thing the speakers agree on.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Move step by step and stop after the last instruction.

lesson.objective: Understand written spoken forms such as gonna, wanna, gotta, I'd and I'll and decide what the speaker will do or wants.

objectives: Understand written spoken forms such as gonna, wanna, gotta, I'd and I'll and decide what the speaker will do or wants.
successCriteria: Understands the speaker's plan, wish or obligation
examples: A: What are you gonna do? B: I'm gonna sleep.
A: I'd better go. I've gotta catch a train.

items.prompt: What does "gonna" mean in "I'm gonna call him"?
items.material: A: Are you gonna call him? B: I'm gonna call him tonight.

items.prompt: What does "gotta" mean in "I gotta leave"?
items.material: A: Stay! B: I can't. I gotta leave at six.

outcomes.studyNotes: Speakers often join words. Gonna means going to. Wanna means want to. Gotta means have got to or have to. Gimme means give me. In writing, you see these forms in informal dialogues, texts and chats. Also notice contractions with 'd. I'd can mean I would: I'd like tea. It can also mean I had: I'd finished. The word after 'd helps: I'd rather means I would rather, and I'd better means I had better, a kind of strong advice. Expand the form in your head, then understand the plan, wish or duty. "I'm gonna stay home" is a plan. "I wanna stay home" is a wish.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Expand informal forms: gonna is going to, wanna is want to, gotta is have to. With 'd check the word after it: rather and like show would, and better shows had.
hints: Say the long form in your head.
Is it a plan, a wish or a duty?
After 'd, look at the next word.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Read the dialogue again and look at the last thing the speakers agree on.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Expand the form, then read the meaning.

outcomes.studyNotes: Attitude is the speaker's feeling about something. In a text dialogue we cannot hear the voice, so we must read the words. Positive words in a negative situation often show sarcasm: "Oh great, another delay" means the speaker is annoyed. Hedges such as I suppose, well, if you really want, and I guess often show reluctance. Strong words like delighted, wonderful, can't wait show real enthusiasm. Worried speakers use what if, I hope, and I am not sure. Ask two questions: what is the situation, and do the words match it? If the words are positive but the situation is bad, the attitude is probably sarcastic.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Compare the words with the situation. Positive words in bad situations are sarcastic. Hedges such as I suppose show reluctance. Strong positive words show real delight.
hints: Is the situation good or bad?
Do the words match the situation?
Look for hedges like I suppose or well.

scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Check whether words and situation match.
